modules.title: Foundations: what a startup really is
modules.outcome: Know what makes a startup different, how expert entrepreneurs think, and the patterns behind failure.

lessons.title: What a startup is — and the stages it goes through
lessons.summary: A startup is a company designed to grow fast, searching for a business model that repeats and scales. It moves through stages, and the right work depends on the stage you are in.
key_ideas: A small business aims to be profitable and stable; a startup aims for fast growth into a large market. Growth is the defining trait.
Early on you are searching, not executing: the business model is a set of guesses to test.
The usual stages are idea, problem-solution fit, MVP traction, product-market fit, and scale. Skipping a stage is the most common way to waste money.
Measure growth weekly or monthly. During an accelerator a good revenue growth rate is roughly 5-7% a week; most companies later aim for 10-20% a month early on.
Each stage has one main question: Is the problem real? Will people pay for this solution? Do they keep using it? Can we acquire customers profitably? Can we do it at scale?

framework.name: Startup stage ladder
steps: Idea — you believe a problem exists
Problem-solution fit — customers confirm the pain and commit to your solution
MVP traction — people use and pay for a first version
Product-market fit — a group of users would be very disappointed without you and keep using it
Scale — a repeatable, profitable acquisition engine; growth becomes an operations problem

checklist: Write down which stage you are in and the evidence for it
Write the one question your stage must answer
Pick the single metric that answers it
pitfalls: Hiring and spending like a scale-up while still at the idea stage
Measuring vanity numbers (downloads, followers) instead of the stage question

quiz.q: What most distinguishes a startup from a small business?
quiz.why: Many companies are new or use technology; a startup is built to grow fast into a large market.

quiz.q: A team with no customer interviews is hiring five engineers. Which stage problem is this?
quiz.why: They are spending like a later stage before proving the problem exists — premature scaling.

sources.title: Paul Graham — Startup = Growth

Steve Blank — Customer Development (The Four Steps to the Epiphany)

rules.says: At the idea stage the only job is to confirm a painful problem for a specific customer.
With a confirmed problem, the next job is to prove people commit to your solution before building much.
With early users and revenue, the job is product-market fit: retention and users who would be very disappointed without you.
After product-market fit, find a repeatable, profitable way to acquire customers.
With fit and working unit economics, scaling the proven engine is the priority.

lessons.title: How expert entrepreneurs think (effectuation)
lessons.summary: Research on expert founders shows they rarely start with a fixed goal and a plan. They start with what they have, limit what they can lose, build partnerships and use surprises.
key_ideas: Bird in hand: start with who you are, what you know and whom you know — not with a perfect idea.
Affordable loss: decide what you can afford to lose instead of forecasting returns you cannot know.
Crazy quilt: people who commit early (customers, partners) shape the venture with you.
Lemonade: treat surprises as information and opportunities, not only as threats.
Pilot in the plane: focus on what you can control; the future is made, not predicted.
checklist: List your means: skills, network, savings, unfair insights
Set your affordable loss in money and months
Name three people who could commit something this week
pitfalls: Waiting for certainty before acting
Betting money or time you cannot afford to lose

quiz.q: 'Affordable loss' means:
options: Decide in advance what you can afford to lose
quiz.why: Experts limit downside to what they can bear rather than chase forecasted upside.

quiz.q: A founder pivots after a customer asks for something unexpected. Which principle is this?
quiz.why: Turning a surprise into an opportunity is the lemonade principle.

lessons.title: Why startups fail — and how to avoid the common traps
lessons.summary: Post-mortems of failed startups show the same causes again and again: building something nobody needs, running out of money, team problems, being out-competed and weak business models.
key_ideas: 'No market need' is the most cited reason in post-mortems (roughly 35-42% across updates of CB Insights' analysis).
Running out of cash or failing to raise is next (roughly 30-38%). Cash is usually the final cause, not the root cause.
Team problems, being out-competed, a poor product, no business model and pricing or cost issues each appear in a meaningful share.
Most failures have several causes; most are visible early if you look at the right evidence.
The defence is the method in this course: validate the problem, test before building, watch unit economics and runway, and agree founder terms early.
checklist: Run a pre-mortem: imagine it failed in 18 months and list why
For each cause, write the earliest warning sign
Put those warning signs on your monthly review
pitfalls: Treating 'we ran out of money' as the cause instead of what led to it
Ignoring co-founder conflict until it is too late

quiz.q: Which reason is most cited in startup post-mortems?
quiz.why: Building something people do not need is consistently the top cause.

quiz.q: What is the best early defence against 'no market need'?
quiz.why: Discovery interviews and demand tests reveal missing need before money is spent.

lessons.title: Finding a problem worth solving
lessons.summary: Great startups start from a real, painful problem, not from a solution. A strong problem statement names who has it, why it matters to them and how it hurts today.
key_ideas: A real problem is ongoing, significant, widespread and largely unaddressed.
Painkillers beat vitamins: people pay to remove pain sooner than to gain a nice-to-have.
Signs of a hair-on-fire problem: people already spend money or time on bad workarounds.
Use the 5 Whys to get past symptoms to the root cause; solving a symptom rarely builds a business.
Write the problem as: [segment] struggles to [job] because [root cause], which costs them [time/money/risk].

steps: What job they are trying to get done
Why it is hard today (root cause)

checklist: Write your problem statement in one sentence
List 3 current workarounds and what they cost
Run the 5 Whys on the problem with a real customer
pitfalls: Starting from a technology and looking for a problem
Describing a problem only you have

options: Friends say it's a great idea
People already pay for clumsy workarounds
quiz.why: Money and time already spent on workarounds prove the pain.

quiz.q: The 5 Whys helps you:

lessons.title: Industries, domains and trends
lessons.summary: An industry is a group of related companies; a domain is a specialised segment inside it. Good opportunities sit where a growing domain meets a change that makes a new solution possible.
key_ideas: Look for 'why now': a new technology, a regulation, a behaviour shift or a cost drop that opens a door.
Judge macro attractiveness: size, growth, margins, fragmentation and how fast buyers adopt new tools.
Use PESTEL (political, economic, social, technological, environmental, legal) to scan for shifts.
Map the ecosystem: suppliers, customers, competitors, regulators and investors all shape what is possible.
In India, digital public infrastructure (UPI, Aadhaar-based KYC, ONDC, Account Aggregator) has created many 'why now' openings.
checklist: Write your 'why now' in one sentence
Run a PESTEL scan for your domain
List the ecosystem players and what each wants
pitfalls: Choosing a shrinking domain because it is familiar
Having no answer to 'why hasn't this been done before?'
india: India's digital public infrastructure (UPI, ONDC, Account Aggregator, DigiLocker) lowers the cost of payments, KYC and distribution for new products.

quiz.q: 'Why now?' asks about:
options: The change that makes the idea possible or urgent today
quiz.why: Investors and founders look for the recent change that opens the opportunity.

quiz.q: A domain is:
options: A specialised segment within an industry
quiz.why: Industries are broad; domains are the specific segments inside them.

lessons.title: Judging ideas: founder-market fit and the scale test
lessons.summary: An idea is worth pursuing when the problem is real, the market can be large, and you are the right people to win it. Judge ideas before falling in love with them.
key_ideas: Founder-market fit: do you have unusual insight, access or skill for this market?
The scale test: could this credibly reach about ₹80 crore (≈$10M) in annual revenue in 3-5 years? If not, it may be a fine small business but a hard venture-backed startup.
Score ideas on pain, market size, founder fit, speed to first revenue and competition.
Prefer ideas where you can reach first customers within weeks.
Ideas are cheap; the evidence you collect about them is what has value.
checklist: Score your top 3 ideas on the scorecard
Do the scale test with rough numbers
Write your unfair insight in one line
pitfalls: Choosing the idea you like most instead of the one with the most evidence
Ignoring that the market is too small to matter

quiz.q: Founder-market fit means:
options: Founders with unusual insight or access for this market
A founder from a top college
quiz.why: It is about why you, specifically, can win this market.

quiz.q: The scale test checks whether:
options: The business could reach a large revenue size in a few years
quiz.why: It is a quick sanity check on market size and business model.

lessons.title: Segmentation and the beachhead market
lessons.summary: You cannot serve everyone at first. Segment the market, pick one beachhead where you can win quickly, and use it as a base to expand.
key_ideas: Segment by demographics, psychographics, behaviour and geography — and for B2B by industry, size and role.
Choose a beachhead where customers are reachable, have money, feel the pain sharply, and talk to each other (word of mouth).
Separate the end user (who uses it) from the economic buyer (who pays) and the other people who influence the decision (the decision-making unit).
Win the beachhead decisively before moving to adjacent markets; dominance in a small market beats a sliver of a big one.
Disciplined Entrepreneurship starts with these steps: segment, pick the beachhead, profile the end user, size the beachhead, define a persona.

steps: You can deliver a complete solution

Map the decision-making unit: user, buyer, influencers, blockers

lessons.title: Jobs to be done and personas
lessons.summary: Customers 'hire' a product to get a job done. Understanding the functional, emotional and social sides of that job tells you what to build and how to talk about it.
key_ideas: Functional job: the practical task (file GST returns on time).
Emotional job: how they want to feel (not anxious about penalties).
Social job: how they want to be seen (a reliable professional to clients).
A persona is a specific, named representative customer: role, day, goals, pains, current tools, and what triggers a purchase.
Build the persona from interview evidence, not imagination.
checklist: Write 3 job statements from interviews
Create one persona with a real name, role and a day in their life
List the 'firing' moment when they look for a new solution
pitfalls: Personas based on stereotypes rather than interviews
Only describing features, never the job

quiz.q: 'I want my clients to see me as dependable' is which kind of job?
quiz.why: How someone wants to be seen by others is the social job.

quiz.q: A persona should be built from:
quiz.why: Personas are only useful when grounded in real conversations.

lessons.title: Customer interviews that tell the truth (the Mom Test)
lessons.summary: Everyone lies to be kind about your idea. Good interviews ask about people's lives and past behaviour, not about your idea or their future intentions.
key_ideas: Talk about their life and problems, not your idea.
Ask about specifics in the past, not generics or opinions about the future.
Talk less, listen more.
Discount compliments, fluff ('I always…', 'I would…') and feature ideas; dig into the motivation behind each request.
Ask for commitment — time, reputation or money. An interview with no next step taught you little.
Do at least 10-15 interviews per segment before deciding; patterns appear around then.

framework.name: Good questions
steps: Tell me about the last time this happened.
What did you do about it?
What does it cost you now?
What have you tried? Why didn't it work?
Who else should I talk to?

checklist: Write 5 past-behaviour questions
Book 15 interviews in one segment
After each, log facts, pains, workarounds and commitments — not compliments
pitfalls: Pitching during the interview
Asking 'would you use this?' or 'how much would you pay?'
Counting compliments as validation

quiz.q: Which is a good Mom Test question?
options: Tell me about the last time you had this problem
quiz.why: It asks about a specific past event, which produces facts instead of polite opinions.

quiz.q: A prospect says 'This is amazing, I'd definitely use it!' This is:
quiz.why: Compliments cost nothing. Look for commitments like time, introductions or money.

rules.says: Fewer than about 10 problem interviews is not enough evidence to build; patterns usually appear after 10-15 conversations per segment.
Interviews without any commitment (time, reputation or money) are weak evidence; ask for a concrete next step or a pre-commitment before building.

modules.title: Validation and the MVP
modules.outcome: Turn assumptions into experiments and build only what you need to learn.

lessons.title: Lean Startup: assumptions and build-measure-learn
lessons.summary: Every plan is a stack of assumptions. The Lean Startup method turns the riskiest ones into fast experiments so you learn before you run out of time and money.
key_ideas: Write your assumptions explicitly: who the customer is, the problem, that they will pay, how you will reach them.
Rank them by risk: how likely they are wrong, and how fatal it would be. Test the riskiest first.
Build-measure-learn: build the smallest thing that tests the assumption, measure behaviour, decide.
Validated learning is the unit of progress early on — not lines of code or features.
Use actionable metrics (that change your decisions), not vanity metrics.

framework.name: Assumption test card
steps: We are right if… (pass threshold set in advance)

checklist: List 10 assumptions behind your plan
Mark the 3 riskiest
Write a test card for the riskiest one with a pass threshold
pitfalls: Setting the success threshold after seeing the results
Testing the easy assumptions instead of the risky ones

options: The one most likely wrong and most fatal if wrong
quiz.why: Riskiest-first saves the most time and money.

quiz.q: Why set the pass threshold before the experiment?

quiz.why: Deciding success criteria upfront prevents rationalising weak results.

lessons.title: Cheap experiments: smoke tests, pre-sales and concierge
lessons.summary: Before building, test demand with experiments that cost days, not months: landing pages, pre-sales, deposits and doing the service by hand.
key_ideas: Landing page smoke test: describe the offer, drive targeted traffic, measure sign-ups and deposits.
Pre-sale or letter of intent: the strongest pre-product evidence is money or a signed commitment.
Concierge MVP: deliver the outcome manually for a few customers to learn what they really need.
Wizard of Oz: the product looks automated, but people do the work behind the scenes.
Set a pass threshold upfront, e.g. 5 paid commitments in 4 weeks.
checklist: Pick one experiment type for your riskiest assumption
Set a budget, a time box and a pass threshold
Run it and record the result honestly
pitfalls: Counting email sign-ups as demand without any cost to the customer
Running tests on friends instead of target customers

quiz.q: Which is the strongest pre-product demand signal?
quiz.why: Money is the clearest commitment.

quiz.q: A concierge MVP means:
options: Delivering the service manually to a few customers
quiz.why: You do it by hand first to learn before automating.

rules.says: Five or more real commitments (pre-orders, deposits, LOIs, paid pilots) are strong evidence of demand; build the smallest product that delivers on them.
A few commitments are encouraging; widen the demand test until you have at least five.

lessons.title: Prototype vs MVP: build to learn
lessons.summary: A prototype tests whether something can work or be understood; an MVP tests whether real users want it. Build the smallest version that delivers the core value once.
key_ideas: Prototype: internal, tests design or feasibility (sketches, clickable mock-ups).
MVP: external, real users, tests demand and value.
Fidelity rises over time: paper → clickable → coded. Do not code what a mock-up can test.
Cut features until it hurts; keep only what delivers the core job.
Time-box the build (4-8 weeks) and decide the success metric before launch.
checklist: List your features and mark the one that delivers the core job
Set a build time box
Write the launch metric and what you will do if it passes or fails
pitfalls: Spending months polishing before any user touches it
Calling a full product an 'MVP'

quiz.q: The main purpose of an MVP is to:
options: Learn whether real users want it with minimum effort
quiz.why: An MVP is a learning tool.

quiz.q: Which is a prototype rather than an MVP?
options: A clickable Figma mock-up shown to the team
An app in the Play Store
quiz.why: A clickable mock-up tests design, not real demand.

rules.says: With interview evidence and some commitments but no MVP, the next step is the smallest MVP that delivers the core job.
Building the full product before about 10 paying customers usually builds features nobody needs; keep the product small until demand is proven.

modules.title: Value and product-market fit
modules.outcome: Quantify your value, recognise product-market fit, and prioritise what to build.

lessons.title: The value proposition — quantified
lessons.summary: Customers buy outcomes, not features. A strong value proposition says what changes for the customer, in numbers they care about.
key_ideas: State value as before vs after: time saved, money saved or earned, risk reduced.
Quantify: '3 hours a week saved' beats 'more efficient'.
Unique value proposition: why you, and not the alternatives — including doing nothing.
Match the value to the persona's top pain and job.
Value sets the ceiling on price; cost sets the floor.
checklist: Write the before/after in numbers
Write your UVP in one sentence
Test it in 5 customer conversations
pitfalls: Listing features instead of outcomes
Claiming value you cannot measure

quiz.q: Which value proposition is strongest?
options: Saves small shops 6 hours of bookkeeping a week
quiz.why: It names a customer and a measurable outcome.

quiz.q: Value relates to price how?
options: Value sets the ceiling, cost the floor
quiz.why: You can charge up to the value delivered; you must charge above cost.

lessons.title: Product-market fit: how to recognise it
lessons.summary: Product-market fit is when a product satisfies a strong market demand: users keep coming back, tell others, and would be very disappointed without it. Before it, everything else is secondary.
key_ideas: Sean Ellis test: ask active users how they would feel if they could no longer use the product. If 40% or more say 'very disappointed', you likely have fit.
Retention curves: plot each monthly cohort. Fit shows as a curve that flattens — a stable share keeps using it — rather than one that falls to zero.
Other signals: organic word of mouth, sales cycles shortening, customers complaining when it breaks.
Below 40%, focus on the users who said 'very disappointed': what they have in common, and what they value most.
Do not scale acquisition before fit; it only fills a leaky bucket.

framework.name: PMF checks
steps: Customers pull, you no longer push

checklist: Survey active users (at least 40 responses if you can)
Plot cohort retention
Interview the 'very disappointed' group
pitfalls: Surveying people who barely used the product
Treating a launch spike as fit

quiz.q: In the Sean Ellis test, the usual product-market fit threshold is:
quiz.why: Around 40% 'very disappointed' is the widely used benchmark.

quiz.q: A retention curve that flattens means:
options: A stable group keeps getting value
quiz.why: A flattening curve shows lasting value for a group of users.

rules.says: 40% or more users 'very disappointed' without the product is the usual sign of product-market fit.
Between about 25% and 40% 'very disappointed' you are close: double down on the users who love it and iterate, before scaling.
Under 25% 'very disappointed' after six months in the market is a strong signal the current direction is not working.
A low score in the first months calls for fast iteration with the users who do care, not yet a pivot.
A retention curve that flattens means a group of users gets lasting value — a core sign of fit.
If cohort retention keeps falling toward zero, more acquisition only fills a leaky bucket; fix retention first.

lessons.title: Roadmaps and prioritisation
lessons.summary: With limited time, what you choose not to build matters as much as what you build. Prioritise by impact on your stage metric.
key_ideas: Tie every item to the stage metric (activation, retention, revenue).
RICE scoring: Reach × Impact × Confidence ÷ Effort.
Talk to customers weekly; let evidence, not the loudest customer, set priorities.
Ship small, often, and measure each release.
Kill features that nobody uses; they slow everything down.

quiz.why: Effort is the divisor, so more effort lowers the score.

modules.outcome: Size your market from the bottom up and position against real alternatives.

lessons.title: Market sizing: TAM, SAM and SOM from the bottom up
lessons.summary: Market size tells you how big the prize is. Build it bottom-up — number of customers × what each pays — rather than quoting a big industry figure.
key_ideas: TAM: total revenue if every possible customer bought.
SAM: the part you can serve with your product, channel and geography.
SOM: what you can realistically win in 2-4 years.
Bottom-up: count reachable customers in the beachhead × annual price. It is more credible than top-down percentages.
Size the beachhead first; then add follow-on markets.
checklist: Count customers in your beachhead with a cited source
Multiply by annual price
Show TAM → SAM → SOM with your assumptions
pitfalls: 'If we get 1% of India…' top-down sizing
Mixing users and paying customers

quiz.q: SOM is:
options: What you can realistically win in a few years
quiz.why: SOM is the obtainable slice in the near term.

quiz.q: Why is bottom-up sizing preferred?
options: It is built from real customer counts and prices, so it is more credible
quiz.why: Bottom-up shows you understand who the customers are and what they pay.

lessons.title: Competition and positioning
lessons.summary: There is always competition — including spreadsheets, WhatsApp and doing nothing. Map it honestly and choose a position where you are clearly better for a specific customer.
key_ideas: Direct competitors: same solution, same customer. Indirect: different solution, same job. Also the status quo.
'We have no competitors' is a red flag to investors: either there is no market or you have not looked.
Position on the two attributes your beachhead customer values most; find the whitespace.
Note each competitor's weakness and the customers it underserves.
Compete on a dimension incumbents cannot easily copy.

Find the empty quadrant you can own

Draw the 2×2 positioning map
Write one sentence on why customers switch to you

Ignoring the status quo as a competitor

quiz.why: A different solution to the same job is indirect competition.

quiz.q: 'We have no competitors' usually signals:
quiz.why: Every real need has some alternative, even doing nothing.

lessons.title: Moats and unfair advantages
lessons.summary: Over time, a business needs something that is hard to copy. Early on it is speed and insight; later it becomes network effects, data, brand, switching costs or scale.
key_ideas: Early moat: speed of learning and closeness to customers.
Network effects: each new user makes the product more valuable for others.
Switching costs: data, workflows and integrations that make leaving painful.
Brand, proprietary data and technology, economies of scale and regulatory licences.
An unfair advantage can't be easily bought: unique insight, access, community or IP.
checklist: Write your current unfair advantage honestly
Pick the moat you will build over 3 years
List the actions that deepen it
pitfalls: Claiming 'first mover' as a moat
Relying on a patent alone in a fast market

quiz.why: Value rising with users is the definition.

quiz.q: The most reliable early-stage advantage is usually:
options: Speed of learning and closeness to customers
quiz.why: Early on, learning faster than others is what you control.

lessons.title: Revenue models and the business model canvas
lessons.summary: A business model describes how you create, deliver and capture value. The Business Model Canvas and Lean Canvas put it on one page so you can see and test each part.
key_ideas: Revenue models: transaction, subscription, freemium, usage-based, marketplace commission, advertising, licensing, services.
Business Model Canvas (9 blocks): customer segments, value propositions, channels, customer relationships, revenue streams, key resources, key activities, key partners, cost structure.
Lean Canvas swaps some blocks for startup risks: problem, solution, key metrics, unfair advantage.
Each block is an assumption to test, not a fact.
Back-of-the-envelope: revenue = price × units; profit = revenue − (setup + fixed + variable costs).

Do the back-of-the-envelope profit maths

Ignoring the cost structure

lessons.title: Pricing on value
lessons.summary: Price is the fastest lever on profit. Price on the value you deliver, test what customers will actually pay, and expect to raise prices as the product improves.
key_ideas: Strategies: cost-plus, value-based, competition-based (penetration or skimming), tiered, usage-based, psychological.
Value-based pricing: charge a fraction of the measurable value you create.
Test willingness to pay by asking for money at different price points, not by asking opinions.
If almost nobody pushes back on price, you are probably too cheap.
Lowering price is rarely the fix; check whether the objection is really about value or fit.
Grandfather existing customers when you raise prices for new ones.

framework.name: Pricing experiment
steps: Measure conversion and revenue per prospect
Keep the price that maximises revenue with healthy margins

checklist: Estimate the value you create per customer per month
Run a 3-price test with real offers
Set a review date for pricing every quarter

rules.says: When most qualified prospects buy and almost nobody pushes back on price, the price is likely too low.

lessons.title: Unit economics: LTV, CAC, payback and margins
lessons.summary: Unit economics tell you whether each customer makes or loses money. Get them right before spending heavily on growth.
key_ideas: CAC (customer acquisition cost) = total sales and marketing spend ÷ new paying customers.
LTV (lifetime value) ≈ monthly revenue per customer × gross margin ÷ monthly churn.
LTV:CAC of at least 3:1 is the common minimum; 4-5:1 is strong.
CAC payback = CAC ÷ (monthly revenue per customer × gross margin). Under 12 months is a clean target; enterprise deals can stretch to 18-24.
Monthly churn of about 3-5% is typical for small-business customers; enterprise churn is often under 1%.
Software gross margins are usually 70-85%; low margins limit everything else.
checklist: Compute CAC per channel, not just blended
Compute LTV with gross margin, not revenue
Set targets: LTV:CAC ≥ 3, payback ≤ 12 months
pitfalls: Computing LTV on revenue instead of gross margin
Using blended CAC that hides a bad paid channel
Assuming churn will improve later

quiz.q: ARPU ₹1,000/month, gross margin 80%, monthly churn 4%. LTV is about:
LTV ₹20,000 and CAC ₹10,000. Should you scale paid spend?
options: Not yet — 2:1 is below the common 3:1 minimum
quiz.why: 2:1 leaves too little after overheads; improve economics first.

rules.says: LTV:CAC below 1 means every new customer loses money; scaling acquisition would multiply losses.
LTV:CAC between 1 and 3 is below the common 3:1 minimum; improve price, margin, churn or CAC before scaling spend.
LTV:CAC of 3:1 or better means customers pay back their acquisition cost several times over; profitable channels can be scaled.
A CAC payback longer than about 18 months ties up cash for too long for an early-stage company.
Payback within 12 months is a clean target: spend comes back within a year.
Monthly churn above about 5% means customers leave faster than most models can sustain; fix retention first.

lessons.title: Traction channels and the Bullseye method

key_ideas: There are about 19 traction channels: e.g. content, SEO, paid search, social ads, PR, community, partnerships, sales, events, affiliates, email, viral loops, offline ads.
Bullseye: brainstorm all channels (outer ring), shortlist the 3 most promising (middle ring), run cheap tests, and focus on the one that works (inner ring).
Each test needs a budget, a time limit and a target CAC.
Match channel to deal size: high-value B2B deals justify direct sales; low-price consumer products need low-cost, scalable channels.
Paid acquisition works only when you know LTV and the payback is short.

lessons.title: Financial basics and a simple model
lessons.summary: You don't need a 40-tab spreadsheet. You need a model that shows revenue, costs and cash month by month, and the few assumptions that drive them.
key_ideas: Three statements: profit and loss (are we profitable?), cash flow (do we have cash?), balance sheet (what we own and owe).
Costs: setup (one-time), fixed (rent, salaries) and variable (per unit: hosting, delivery, payment fees). COGS are the direct costs of delivering.
Model drivers, not outputs: leads × conversion × price; customers × churn.
Profit is not cash: GST, receivables and inventory can drain cash even when profitable.
Keep a base, downside and upside case.
checklist: Build a 24-month monthly model from 5-8 drivers
Add a downside case with half the growth
Reconcile it with your bank balance monthly
pitfalls: Hockey-stick revenue with flat costs
Forgetting taxes, GST and payment delays
india: Plan for GST timing: you may pay GST on invoices before customers pay you.
Budget for statutory costs: company filings, audit, TDS and professional fees.

quiz.q: A company can be profitable but run out of cash because:

lessons.title: Burn, runway and default alive
lessons.summary: Runway is how many months you can survive. Default alive asks whether, on current growth and spending, you reach profitability before the money runs out.
key_ideas: Net burn = monthly spend − monthly revenue. Runway = cash ÷ net burn.
Default alive: with current revenue growth and constant costs, revenue catches up with costs before cash runs out. Default dead: it doesn't.
Fundraising usually takes 3-6 months; start with about 9-12 months of runway left, not 3.
Below about 6 months of runway, cutting burn becomes urgent; below 3, it is an emergency.
Burn multiple = net burn ÷ net new revenue. Under about 1.5 is efficient; above 2 is concerning.
checklist: Calculate runway with a 3-month average burn
Answer default alive or dead
Set the runway level that triggers fundraising or cuts
pitfalls: Assuming the next round will arrive in time
Hiring ahead of revenue with under 12 months of runway

quiz.q: Cash ₹30 lakh, net burn ₹5 lakh/month. Runway is:
quiz.why: 30 ÷ 5 = 6 months.

quiz.q: When should you usually start fundraising?
quiz.why: Raising takes months; start while you have time.

sources.title: Paul Graham — Default Alive or Default Dead?

rules.says: Under 3 months of runway is an emergency: cut burn immediately; a normal fundraise takes longer than the cash lasts.
With 3-6 months of runway, cut burn now and raise in parallel; fundraising takes 3-6 months.
With 6-12 months of runway and not default alive, start fundraising now — it takes 3-6 months.
18+ months of runway gives room to execute; keep a monthly cash review.
Default alive: on current growth and costs you reach profitability before cash runs out, so you can raise from strength — or not at all.
Default dead: on the current path the money runs out first; change something — costs, revenue or funding — now.
A burn multiple above 2 means you burn more than ₹2 for each ₹1 of new revenue — inefficient growth.
A burn multiple of 1 or lower is efficient growth.

lessons.title: Bootstrapping and cash discipline
lessons.summary: Many great companies are funded by customers first. Cash discipline gives you time, options and better terms if you raise later.
key_ideas: Customer funding: annual plans paid upfront, deposits, paid pilots, services that fund product.
Keep fixed costs low; prefer variable costs early.
Every rupee should either build the product customers want or bring in revenue.
Negotiate: payment terms, startup credits for cloud and tools, shared spaces.
Bootstrapping until a milestone can raise valuation and reduce dilution later.
checklist: Offer annual prepaid plans with a discount
Apply for cloud and tool startup credits
Review every subscription monthly
pitfalls: Spending on brand and office before customers
Taking any money at any terms out of panic

quiz.q: Which is customer funding?
quiz.why: Customers pay before you deliver, funding growth.

quiz.q: Early on, prefer costs that are:
quiz.why: Variable costs fall when revenue does, protecting runway.

lessons.title: The funding ladder: when and from whom to raise
lessons.summary: Funding comes in steps — own savings, friends and family, grants, angels, seed VCs, then larger rounds. Each step funds a specific milestone and expects specific evidence.
key_ideas: Raise to reach a milestone that makes the company more valuable, not to 'have money'.
Sources: bootstrapping and customers, friends and family, grants and government schemes, angels and angel networks, accelerators, seed and venture funds, debt.
Investors fund evidence: traction, growth rate, retention, and a team that can win.
Non-dilutive money (grants, schemes, credits) costs no equity — use what you are eligible for.
Debt suits companies with steady revenue that can repay.
Venture capital suits businesses that can grow very large; many good businesses should not take VC.

Calculate amount = 18-24 months of planned burn
List grants and schemes you qualify for
pitfalls: Raising before you can show any evidence
Raising too little to reach the next milestone
india: Government options include the Startup India Seed Fund Scheme (via incubators), state startup policy grants, and the Fund of Funds that backs SEBI-registered funds.

You appear eligible for the Startup India Seed Fund Scheme (grant up to ₹20 lakh, debt or convertible up to ₹50 lakh via incubators); apply before you turn two.

lessons.title: Instruments and terms in India: equity, CCPS, SAFEs, notes and CCDs
lessons.summary: How you raise matters as much as how much. In India, the instrument decides the paperwork, who can invest, and what happens at conversion. Always use a lawyer.
key_ideas: Equity shares or CCPS (compulsorily convertible preference shares) at an agreed valuation are the standard for priced rounds; investors usually get CCPS.
US-style SAFEs are not directly recognised in India; India-adapted versions (e.g. iSAFE) are usually structured as CCPS with a valuation cap and discount.
Convertible notes: only DPIIT-recognised startups can issue them; at least ₹25 lakh per investor in a single tranche; repay or convert within 10 years; the investor can choose repayment.
CCDs (compulsorily convertible debentures): any private company can issue them; they must convert; a special resolution and usually a valuation report are needed.
Foreign investment follows FEMA pricing and reporting rules through your bank.
Key terms: valuation (pre/post-money), cap, discount, liquidation preference, anti-dilution, board seats, ESOP pool.
Angel tax (Section 56(2)(viib)) was abolished for all classes of investors from FY 2024-25, removing a long-standing worry for early rounds.

DPIIT startup and ₹25L+ per investor? → convertible note is possible
Otherwise, CCD with a valuation report

Check DPIIT status before considering notes
Get legal and valuation advice before signing

Ignoring the dilution from the ESOP pool and conversion caps

lessons.summary: A raise is a sales process: a clear story, a target list, a tight timeline and many conversations. The deck gets the meeting; traction and the team close it.

Know your numbers cold: growth, CAC, LTV, churn, runway, use of funds.

lessons.title: Co-founders, equity splits and vesting
lessons.summary: Co-founder conflict is one of the most common reasons startups die. Agree roles, equity and vesting in writing at the start, while everyone is still friends.
key_ideas: Pick co-founders for complementary skills, shared values and proven ability to work together.
Split equity on future contribution, not on who had the idea; equal splits are common when commitment is equal.
Always vest: the usual standard is 4 years with a 1-year cliff, so a founder who leaves early does not keep a large stake.
Write a founders' agreement: roles, vesting, IP assignment to the company, decision-making, deadlock and exit terms.
Part-time founders usually vest from when they go full-time, or get a smaller share.

Agree the split and 4-year vesting with 1-year cliff
Sign IP assignment for all founders

lessons.title: Hiring the first team and ESOPs
lessons.summary: Early hires shape the company's culture and speed. Hire slowly, for ownership and learning speed, and use stock options to align people with the long term.

Set up an ESOP plan before your first key hire

lessons.title: Choosing a legal entity in India
lessons.summary: Your entity decides liability, compliance cost, and whether investors can invest. Most startups that plan to raise equity choose a private limited company.
key_ideas: Sole proprietorship: quickest; no separate legal identity; unlimited personal liability; cannot take equity investment.
Partnership firm: two or more partners; unlimited liability unless an LLP.
LLP: limited liability, lighter compliance; good for services; cannot issue equity shares or a standard ESOP plan, so VCs rarely invest.
One Person Company (OPC): a company with a single owner; limited liability; convert when you add co-founders or investors.
Private limited company: separate legal entity, limited liability, can issue shares and ESOPs — the standard for venture-backed startups. Incorporate via the MCA SPICe+ form.
Choose for where you are going: converting later costs time and money.

framework.name: Entity chooser
steps: Raising equity or giving ESOPs? → Private limited
Services, no outside equity, 2+ owners? → LLP
Solo, not raising yet? → OPC or proprietorship
Testing an idea with no revenue? → you may not need an entity yet

lessons.title: DPIIT recognition, tax benefits and GST
lessons.summary: DPIIT recognition unlocks most Startup India benefits. Know the 2026 eligibility rules, the tax holiday, and when GST registration becomes mandatory.
key_ideas: DPIIT startup definition (notified 4 February 2026, G.S.R. 108(E)): up to 10 years from incorporation and turnover not above ₹200 crore in any year; deep-tech startups up to 20 years and ₹300 crore.

Eligible entities: private limited companies, registered partnership firms, LLPs and (newly) multi-state and state cooperative societies. The business must work on innovation or a scalable model with potential for jobs or wealth.
Benefits include self-certification for several labour and environment laws, faster patent examination with fee rebates, easier public procurement norms, and access to schemes like SISFS and CGSS.

Section 80-IAC tax holiday: 100% deduction of profits for any 3 consecutive years out of the first 10, for DPIIT-recognised private companies and LLPs incorporated by 31 March 2030, with turnover up to ₹100 crore in the claim year and an Inter-Ministerial Board certificate.
Angel tax was abolished for all investors from FY 2024-25.

GST registration: services above ₹20 lakh turnover (₹10 lakh in special category states); goods above ₹40 lakh where the state has opted in (₹20 lakh in special category states). Registration is mandatory regardless of turnover for inter-state supply of goods, e-commerce sellers and some other cases.

If profitable soon, plan the 80-IAC application
Track turnover against GST thresholds; register before you cross them
pitfalls: Missing GST registration for inter-state goods sales
Assuming tax and scheme figures never change
india: Figures checked November 2026. The new Income-tax Act, 2025 renumbers many sections; confirm current section numbers and conditions with a CA.
Special category states for GST thresholds include Arunachal Pradesh, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Sikkim, Tripura and Uttarakhand.

lessons.title: Government schemes and the startup ecosystem
lessons.summary: India has a large support system for startups: seed grants, credit guarantees, funds of funds, incubators and mentors. Knowing what you qualify for can save months and equity.

SISFS eligibility: DPIIT-recognised; not more than 2 years old at application; private limited, LLP or registered partnership; not more than ₹10 lakh of prior government monetary support.
Credit Guarantee Scheme for Startups (CGSS): cover up to ₹20 crore per borrower — 85% for loans up to ₹10 crore, 75% above — with a reduced 1% fee for champion sectors.
Fund of Funds for Startups: the government invests in SEBI-registered funds that invest in startups; Budget 2025 announced a new ₹10,000 crore fund of funds.
Budget 2025 also announced term loans up to ₹2 crore for first-time women, SC and ST entrepreneurs.
Incubators (university, government and corporate), accelerators, state startup missions and the MAARG mentorship portal add mentoring and networks.
checklist: List the schemes you qualify for today
Shortlist 3 incubators that run SISFS in your sector
Check your state's startup policy for grants and reimbursements
pitfalls: Missing the SISFS two-year window
Applying with a weak business plan or no prototype evidence

modules.title: Decisions and strategy
modules.outcome: Make better decisions under uncertainty: when to pivot, when to scale, and how to think clearly.

lessons.title: Decision-making under uncertainty
lessons.summary: Founders make hundreds of decisions with incomplete information. Good process — not perfect information — is what improves results over time.
key_ideas: One-way vs two-way doors: decide reversible choices fast; slow down for irreversible ones (a framing popularised by Amazon's 2015 shareholder letter).
Write the decision, options, evidence and expected outcome before deciding; review later (a decision journal).
Pre-mortem: imagine the decision failed and list why — it surfaces risks people hesitate to raise.
Judge decisions by the process and information available, not only by outcome (luck plays a part).
Decide with the data you have when waiting costs more than being wrong; name what would change your mind.
Separate facts, assumptions and opinions in every discussion.
checklist: Start a decision journal
Run a 15-minute pre-mortem on your next big decision
Review decisions monthly against outcomes
pitfalls: Treating every decision as irreversible
Judging a good decision as bad because of bad luck

quiz.q: A 'two-way door' decision is one that:
quiz.why: Reversible decisions should be made quickly.

quiz.q: A pre-mortem asks the team to:
options: Imagine the project failed and explain why
quiz.why: It surfaces risks before they happen.

sources.title: Gary Klein — Performing a Project Premortem (HBR)

lessons.title: Pivot or persevere
lessons.summary: Every startup reaches moments where the plan isn't working. Decide on evidence, at a set time, and if you pivot, keep what you learned.
key_ideas: Schedule pivot-or-persevere reviews (e.g. every 8-12 weeks) instead of deciding in a panic.
Signals to persevere: improving retention, a group of users who love the product, growth in the key metric.
Signals to pivot: flat metrics after several real iterations, weak Sean Ellis scores, customers who like it but won't pay.
Pivot types: zoom-in (one feature becomes the product), customer segment, customer need, platform, business model, channel, technology.
A pivot changes one fundamental part of the plan while keeping what you learned.
With little runway and weak signals, consider pausing or winding down responsibly.
checklist: Set the next pivot-or-persevere date
Write the metric thresholds for each outcome now
List what you have learned that stays true after any pivot
pitfalls: Endless small tweaks with no decision
Pivoting so often nothing is tested properly

quiz.q: A 'zoom-in' pivot means:
options: Turning one feature into the whole product
quiz.why: A single valued feature becomes the product.

quiz.q: Why schedule pivot-or-persevere reviews in advance?
options: To decide on evidence instead of in a panic
quiz.why: A set review with thresholds avoids emotional decisions.

sources.title: Eric Ries — The Lean Startup principles

rules.says: Little or no growth after nine months in market usually means the current plan needs a fundamental change.
Revenue growing 10%+ month on month is a strong reason to persevere.
Weak traction with under 3 months of runway: plan a responsible pause or wind-down, or a drastic pivot you can afford.

lessons.title: When and how to scale
lessons.summary: Scaling too early is a top cause of failure; scaling too late lets competitors win. Scale when the engine is proven, then build the organisation around it.
key_ideas: Scale when you have product-market fit, LTV:CAC of 3+ and a channel that pays back predictably.
Premature scaling: hiring, spending and expanding before fit — it multiplies burn without multiplying learning.
Crossing the chasm: early adopters are not the mainstream; you need references and a complete solution for a focused segment to cross.
Build systems: playbooks, metrics dashboards, managers for functions founders still run.
Expand to adjacent segments one at a time from your beachhead.
Protect culture and unit economics as you grow.
checklist: Check the scale gate: PMF, LTV:CAC ≥ 3, payback ≤ 12-18 months
Write the playbook for your main channel
Pick the next adjacent segment
pitfalls: Expanding to new cities or segments before the first one works
Hiring faster than you can onboard

quiz.q: Which is a sign you're ready to scale?
options: PMF plus LTV:CAC of 3+ and a predictable channel
quiz.why: Scale a proven engine, not a hope.

quiz.q: 'Crossing the chasm' refers to moving from:
options: Early adopters to the mainstream market
quiz.why: Mainstream buyers need references and complete solutions.

glossary.ARPU: Average revenue per user or customer, usually per month.
glossary.CAC: Customer acquisition cost: sales and marketing spend divided by new paying customers.
glossary.LTV: Lifetime value: the gross profit a customer brings over their lifetime.
glossary.Churn: The share of customers (or revenue) lost in a period.
glossary.Runway: Months until cash runs out at the current net burn.
glossary.Burn multiple: Net burn divided by net new revenue in the same period.
glossary.MVP: Minimum viable product: the smallest product that tests whether real users want it.
glossary.PMF: Product-market fit: a product that satisfies strong demand, shown by retention and user love.
glossary.TAM / SAM / SOM: Total, serviceable and obtainable market sizes.
glossary.DPIIT: Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade, which recognises startups under Startup India.
glossary.SISFS: Startup India Seed Fund Scheme: grants and debt for early startups through incubators.
glossary.CGSS: Credit Guarantee Scheme for Startups: government guarantees on loans to DPIIT startups.
glossary.CCPS: Compulsorily convertible preference shares: the usual instrument for investors in Indian startups.
glossary.CCD: Compulsorily convertible debentures: debentures that must convert to equity.
glossary.Vesting: Earning shares over time, so people who leave early don't keep all their equity.
glossary.Beachhead: The first focused market segment you aim to dominate.
glossary.JTBD: Jobs to be done: the progress a customer is trying to make.

focus.label: What to focus on next
examples: What should I focus on next?
What is my priority this month?

options.label: Find a problem worth solving
options.summary: Talk to customers until you can state a painful, frequent, unsolved problem for a specific segment.

options.label: Validate the solution before building
options.summary: Prove people want your solution by getting commitments (time, reputation or money) before you build much.

options.label: Reach product-market fit
options.summary: Iterate with your users until retention flattens and 40%+ would be very disappointed without you.

options.label: Build a repeatable growth engine
options.summary: Find one or two channels that bring customers profitably and predictably.

options.label: Scale what works
options.summary: Pour resources into the proven engine while protecting unit economics and culture.

build_or_validate.label: Build now or validate first
examples: Should we start building the app now?
Is it time to build the MVP?

options.label: Do customer discovery first
options.summary: You do not yet know enough about the problem; building now risks making something nobody needs.

options.label: Run a cheap demand test
options.summary: The problem looks real; now test if people will commit to your solution before you build it.

options.label: Build the smallest MVP
options.summary: You have evidence of demand; build the smallest product that tests the riskiest assumption with real users.

options.label: Build the full product
options.summary: Build the complete product. Right only when demand is proven and the MVP is limiting growth.

pivot_or_persevere.label: Pivot or persevere
examples: Should we pivot?
Is it time to change direction?

options.label: Persevere
options.summary: The signals are good enough; keep going and focus on the bottleneck.

options.label: Iterate (change one thing)
options.summary: There are real signals but not enough; change one variable (segment, feature, price, channel) and measure.

options.label: Pivot
options.summary: The current direction is not working; keep what you learned and change a fundamental part of the plan.

options.label: Pause or wind down
options.summary: Low traction and little runway left; protect people and money and decide calmly.

pricing.label: Pricing
examples: Should we raise our prices?
How should we price the product?

options.label: Raise prices
options.summary: Signals say you are under-priced; raise prices for new customers and watch conversion.

options.label: Run a pricing experiment
options.summary: You do not yet know what customers will pay; test price points against the value you deliver.

options.label: Keep current pricing
options.summary: Price is working; spend energy elsewhere.

options.label: Lower prices
options.summary: Price is the real blocker for a price-sensitive segment. Rarely the right first move.

scale_growth.label: Spend on growth
examples: Should we spend more on ads to grow?
Is it time to scale marketing?

options.label: Scale paid acquisition
options.summary: Unit economics work; increase spend on the channels that pay back.

options.label: Fix unit economics first
options.summary: Each customer costs more than they return; scaling would multiply losses.

options.label: Improve retention first
options.summary: Customers leave too fast; fix the leaky bucket before pouring in more.

options.label: Keep testing channels
options.summary: You have not yet found a channel that works predictably.

channel.label: Go-to-market channel
examples: How do we get our first customers?
Which marketing channel should we use?

options.label: Founder-led sales
options.summary: Founders sell directly: outreach, demos, closing. Best for B2B and for the first customers of any startup.

options.label: Content and community
options.summary: Build trust and organic demand where your customers already gather.

options.label: Paid acquisition
options.summary: Buy attention with ads. Works only when you know LTV and the payback is short.

options.label: Partnerships and distribution
options.summary: Reach customers through someone who already has them.

fundraise_timing.label: Whether to raise money now
examples: Should we raise a seed round now?
Do we need investors?

options.label: Start raising now
options.summary: You have the evidence investors fund (traction, growth) or you must raise to survive; start the process now.

options.label: Build traction first
options.summary: Investors fund evidence. Get more proof first so you raise on better terms, or never need to.

options.label: Use non-dilutive money first
options.summary: Grants and schemes give money without giving up equity; use them while you are eligible.

options.label: Take a loan
options.summary: Debt suits businesses with steady revenue that can repay; it keeps equity.

funding_instrument.label: Funding instrument
examples: Should we use a SAFE or a convertible note?
What instrument should our angel round use?

options.label: Priced equity round (equity shares or CCPS at a set valuation)
options.summary: Investors buy shares at an agreed valuation. Clear ownership; more legal work and a valuation report.

options.label: India-style SAFE (CCPS-based, e.g. iSAFE)
options.summary: Shares that convert later at a cap or discount; quick for small angel rounds without agreeing a valuation today.

options.label: Convertible note
options.summary: Debt that converts to equity later. In India only DPIIT-recognised startups can issue it, with at least ₹25 lakh per investor in one tranche.

options.label: Compulsorily convertible debentures (CCD)
options.summary: Debentures that must convert to equity; any private company can issue them, usually with a valuation report.

runway_burn.label: Runway and burn
examples: We have 5 months of cash, what do we do?
Should we cut costs?

options.label: Cut burn now
options.summary: Reduce spending to buy time; the cheapest money is the money you do not spend.

options.label: Raise a bridge
options.summary: Raise a small round from existing investors to reach the next milestone.

options.label: Push revenue
options.summary: Grow revenue faster: sell to existing customers, raise prices, collect payments sooner.

options.label: Stay the course
options.summary: Runway and trajectory are healthy; keep executing.

hiring.label: Hiring
examples: Should we hire a full-time developer?
Do we need a marketing hire?

options.label: Hire full-time
options.summary: The role is core and you can afford it for a year; hire a strong, committed person.

options.label: Use a contractor or freelancer
options.summary: Get the work done without a long commitment; good for non-core or uncertain work.

options.label: Founders do it for now
options.summary: Before product-market fit, founders learn the most by doing the work themselves.

options.label: Delay the hire
options.summary: Not needed yet or not affordable; revisit at the next milestone.

cofounder_equity.label: Co-founder equity
examples: How should we split equity between co-founders?
Do we need vesting?

options.label: Equal split with vesting
options.summary: Founders who will contribute equally from here split equally, with 4-year vesting and a 1-year cliff.

options.label: Weighted split with vesting
options.summary: Contributions differ (time, role, risk); split to reflect future contribution, still with vesting.

options.label: Split without vesting
options.summary: Shares fully owned from day one. Risky: a founder who leaves keeps everything.

legal_entity.label: Legal entity
examples: Should we register as a private limited company or an LLP?
Which company type should we choose?

options.label: Private limited company
options.summary: The standard for startups that will raise equity or give ESOPs.

options.label: Limited liability partnership (LLP)
options.summary: Limited liability with lighter compliance; good for services firms that will not raise equity.

options.label: Sole proprietorship or partnership
options.summary: Fastest and cheapest, but unlimited liability and no equity investment.

options.label: One person company (OPC)
options.summary: A company with a single owner; limited liability for a solo founder who is not raising yet.
